title: Dedication
hookLine: the good of five years given away to all beings
tomorrow: the teacher is dying. who teaches after him?

lines: MAY THIS BE FOR OUR RELATIVES.
cards: After a big win, some players point up at the stands: that one was for my grandmother. Buddhists have an older version. The commentary on a short text, the Tirokudda Sutta, tells it.
King Bimbisara gave the Buddha and his monks a meal, and that night he heard wailing around the palace: relatives of his who had died, waiting outside the walls, hoping for a share.

The next day he gave again, and this time he dedicated the gift to them. The sutta's own words are simple: may this be for our relatives; may our relatives be happy. So can you give away the good you've done?

teach.b: Buddhists say yes, and they disagree, warmly, about how. Here are the two voices. The first starts from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words: "Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another."
Karma isn't money, this side says; it can't be wired into someone else's account. So what does a dedication do? It invites.
When the departed, or anyone, learns of the good deed and rejoices in it, that gladness is a good act of their own.
In Pali the rejoicing is anumodana, and in Theravada temples you may hear people say sadhu, sadhu, well done, when a gift is offered.
The second voice, strong in the Mahayana, says: giving the good away is generosity too, and generosity grows the good instead of spending it.
Shantideva ends his guide to the bodhisattva's way with a whole chapter of dedication, giving the good he has made to the sick, the frightened, beings in every kind of pain.
And at Mai's family's chùa, as in other Mahayana temples, the chanting ends by dedicating its good to all beings. Two explanations.
In both schools, a good deed can end by being given away: the good isn't kept, it's sent out.

how: Buddhists may end chanting, a meditation, a gift or a memorial by dedicating its merit to others, often to departed relatives and to all beings; in Theravada communities others share by rejoicing (anumodana), often saying 'sadhu'.

o: the blessing of a new temple before it first opens
giving away the good your practice made, so others share it
a vow to keep up your practice every day without fail

games.q: two voices, one practice — tap the pairs.
p: dedicated a meal to his departed relatives
ended his guide with a chapter of dedication
well done: said when a gift is offered

s: dedicating merit means the monks pay off a dead person's bad karma
neither voice says that. one says the departed share by rejoicing; the other, that giving the good away is generosity that grows it.
the Dhammapada says no one can purify another
that verse is why some Buddhists explain dedication through rejoicing, not transfer.
the Tirokudda Sutta is in the Pali canon, and Theravada communities dedicate merit too, often to departed relatives.

games.q: your cousin says, 'karma is your own. dedicating merit is wishful thinking.' you want to give the best case for dedicating anyway, from inside the tradition. what do you say?
o: giving the good away is generosity, and whoever rejoices in it makes good of their own.
merit works like money: the temple can move it into anyone's account.
the Dhammapada says someone else can purify you if they try hard enough.
games.why: both voices in the tradition agree on this much: rejoicing is a good act of one's own, and giving the good away is itself giving.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up. Bring to mind five years of mornings, every sit, every kind word, every page you read.
Then turn your palms over, and give all of it away, silently: to someone you love, to someone who has died, to someone you'll never meet, and then to every being, with no one kept out.

wordCard.voice: Dedication: giving away the good your practice has made, so others may share in it. In Pali, pattidana, the giving of a share.

orig.note: Pali: pattidana, the giving of a share; the dedication of merit.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: may it be shared, the good of today and of five years with it. Eleven days up the summit.

sources.ref: Khuddakapatha 7 (Tirokudda Sutta), also Petavatthu 1.5; the Bimbisara story from its commentary

sources.q: Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another.
